description: Region guides for single-pain insights. The rules layer scores each guide's contributors against what the person logged (pain type, triggers they ticked, words in their notes, pattern, age, sex, recurrence, health data, answers to follow-up questions) and passes the ranked candidates to Claude, which may only explain within them. Wording is deliberately 'often linked to', never a diagnosis.

health_signals.low_sleep: average sleep in the 3 days before onset ≥15% below usual
health_signals.low_hrv: average HRV in the 3 days before onset ≥15% below usual
health_signals.workout_spike: workout minutes in the 3 days before onset ≥50% above usual

sources.nice_low_back: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s
sources.si_joint: Fortin JD et al. Sacroiliac joint pain referral maps. Spine. 1994.
sources.hip_referral: Lesher JM et al. Hip joint pain referral patterns. Pain Med. 2008.
sources.hip_knee: Powers CM. The influence of abnormal hip mechanics on knee injury. JOSPT. 2010.
sources.plantar_heel: Martin RL et al. Heel pain / plantar fasciitis clinical practice guideline. JOSPT. 2014.

general_contributors.name: Short or poor sleep
general_contributors.explanation: Nights with less sleep than usual lower the body's pain tolerance and slow recovery, so pain often flares after them.

general_contributors.name: Lower recovery (HRV) than usual
general_contributors.explanation: Heart rate variability below your usual level often means the body is less recovered, which is commonly linked to more pain and slower healing.

general_contributors.name: A jump in activity
general_contributors.explanation: A sudden increase in training or activity is one of the most common reasons for new muscle and tendon pain.

general_contributors.name: Stress
general_contributors.explanation: Stress makes muscles tense and the nervous system more sensitive, so pain often feels stronger when you're stressed.

guides.title: Head

contributors.name: Tight neck and shoulder muscles
contributors.explanation: Tension in the muscles at the back of the neck and across the shoulders commonly spreads up into the head, especially the back of the head and temples.
contributors.ask: Do your neck or shoulders feel tight or sore too?

contributors.name: Short or poor sleep
contributors.explanation: Headaches are often linked to nights with too little or broken sleep.
contributors.ask: Have you slept less or worse than usual lately?

contributors.name: Eye strain from screens
contributors.explanation: Long stretches of close screen work are commonly linked to aching around the forehead and temples.
contributors.ask: Does it build up during long screen sessions?

contributors.name: Jaw clenching
contributors.explanation: The jaw muscles run up to the temples, so clenching or grinding often shows up as temple ache.
contributors.ask: Do you clench your jaw or grind your teeth?

contributors.name: Not enough water or skipped meals
contributors.explanation: Dehydration and long gaps between meals are common, simple contributors to headaches.
contributors.ask: Have you been drinking less or skipping meals?

contributors.name: Stress
contributors.explanation: Stress tends to tighten the head, neck and jaw muscles and is one of the most common headache triggers.

self_care: Take regular breaks from screens and look into the distance for a minute
Drink some water and eat regularly
Try gentle neck and shoulder stretches, or warmth on the back of the neck
Keep sleep and wake times regular
avoid: Long unbroken screen sessions
Skipping meals
see_someone_if: Headaches are becoming more frequent or different from your usual
It started after a knock to the head
It doesn't ease within a few days

guides.title: Jaw

contributors.name: Clenching or grinding
contributors.explanation: Clenching or grinding the teeth, often at night or under stress, overworks the jaw muscles and is one of the most common causes of jaw pain.
contributors.ask: Is it worse when you wake up, or do you notice clenching?

contributors.name: Jaw joint (TMJ) irritation
contributors.explanation: The joint in front of the ear can get irritated from overuse, often with clicking, tenderness or pain when opening wide.
contributors.ask: Does your jaw click, lock or hurt when you open wide?

contributors.name: Forward-head posture
contributors.explanation: When the head sits forward of the shoulders, the jaw and neck muscles work harder, which is commonly linked to jaw ache.
contributors.ask: Do you spend long periods at a desk or looking down at a phone?

contributors.name: A tooth or gum problem
contributors.explanation: Pain from a tooth or gum can feel like jaw pain, especially if it's worse with hot, cold or sweet food.
contributors.ask: Is one tooth sensitive to hot, cold or biting?

contributors.name: Ear or sinus irritation
contributors.explanation: Ear and sinus problems often feel like pain around the jaw joint, especially with a cold or blocked nose.
contributors.ask: Any cold, blocked nose or ear discomfort?

self_care: Rest the jaw: soft foods for a few days, avoid gum and wide yawns
Warmth on the side of the face can ease the muscles
Notice clenching during the day and let the teeth rest apart
Check your posture at a desk or on your phone
avoid: Chewing gum or very chewy food
Biting nails or pens
see_someone_if: Your jaw locks or you can't open it properly
It lasts more than two weeks
A tooth is involved (see a dentist)
guides.specialist: Dentist (for clenching or TMJ) or physical therapist

guides.title: Neck

contributors.name: Desk or phone posture
contributors.explanation: Long periods looking down or forward load the neck muscles and are one of the most common reasons for neck pain.
contributors.ask: Is it worse after long desk or phone sessions?

contributors.name: Sleeping position or pillow
contributors.explanation: Waking with a stiff, sore neck is commonly linked to an awkward sleeping position or an unsupportive pillow.
contributors.ask: Was it there when you woke up?

contributors.name: Muscle strain
contributors.explanation: A sudden movement, lifting or sport can strain the neck muscles, causing pain and stiffness when turning the head.
contributors.ask: Did it start after a sudden movement, lifting or sport?

contributors.name: Irritated nerve in the neck
contributors.explanation: Pain that travels into the shoulder or arm, or comes with tingling or numbness, is often linked to an irritated nerve root in the neck.
contributors.ask: Does it travel into your shoulder, arm or hand, or come with tingling?

contributors.name: Stress and tension
contributors.explanation: Stress tends to tighten the muscles across the top of the shoulders and neck.

self_care: Keep the neck moving gently: slow turns and tilts within comfort
Warmth across the neck and shoulders
Raise your screen to eye level and take regular breaks
Try a lower or firmer pillow
avoid: Holding one position for a long time
Carrying heavy bags on one shoulder
see_someone_if: It spreads into your arm with tingling or weakness
It doesn't improve after 2 weeks
It started after a fall or accident

guides.title: Shoulder

contributors.name: Irritated shoulder tendons (rotator cuff)
contributors.explanation: The tendons around the shoulder commonly get irritated from repeated overhead movements, often hurting when lifting the arm or lying on that side.
contributors.ask: Does it hurt to lift your arm out to the side or overhead?

contributors.name: Rounded-shoulder posture
contributors.explanation: Sitting with rounded shoulders narrows the space for the shoulder tendons and loads the muscles around the shoulder blade.
contributors.ask: Do you spend long periods at a desk?

contributors.name: Pain coming from the neck
contributors.explanation: Neck problems commonly refer pain to the top and outside of the shoulder, especially with tingling down the arm.
contributors.ask: Is your neck stiff or sore too?

contributors.name: Muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Lifting, pushing or a sudden pull can strain the muscles around the shoulder.
contributors.ask: Did it start after lifting, pushing or a sudden pull?

contributors.name: Shoulder stiffness
contributors.explanation: A shoulder that steadily stiffens over weeks, with pain at night, is worth having checked, especially from middle age.
contributors.ask: Is it getting harder to move your arm over weeks?

self_care: Keep the shoulder moving gently within comfort, e.g. pendulum swings
Ice for 15 minutes after activity, or warmth for stiffness
Sit tall with shoulders relaxed and screen at eye level
Sleep on the other side with a pillow to hug
avoid: Repeated overhead reaching or lifting
Sleeping on the sore side
see_someone_if: You can't lift your arm
It started after a fall
Pain at night keeps getting worse
No improvement after 2 weeks

guides.title: Upper and mid back

contributors.name: Desk or phone posture
contributors.explanation: Hunching forward for long periods loads the muscles between and around the shoulder blades and is one of the most common reasons for upper-back ache.
contributors.ask: Is it worse after long periods sitting or looking at a screen?

contributors.name: Muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Lifting, twisting or sport can strain the muscles of the upper back, often with a sharp catch on certain movements.
contributors.ask: Did it start after lifting, twisting or sport?

contributors.name: Stiff rib joint
contributors.explanation: The small joints where the ribs meet the spine can get stiff and irritated, often hurting with deep breaths or twisting.
contributors.ask: Does it catch when you breathe in deeply or twist?

contributors.name: Stress and tension
contributors.explanation: Stress tightens the muscles across the shoulders and upper back.

contributors.name: Sleeping position
contributors.explanation: An awkward position overnight commonly leaves the upper back stiff in the morning.
contributors.ask: Is it worst when you first wake up?

self_care: Gentle movement: shoulder rolls and slow upper-back twists
Warmth on the sore area
Break up sitting every 30–45 minutes
Set your screen at eye level
avoid: Long slumped sitting
Heavy lifting until it settles
see_someone_if: It came with chest pain, breathlessness or sweating (call emergency services)
It started after a fall
No improvement after 2 weeks

guides.title: Chest

contributors.name: Chest-wall muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Exercise, lifting or heavy coughing can strain the muscles between the ribs, often sore to press and worse with movement.
contributors.ask: Is it sore when you press on it or move your arms?

contributors.name: Irritated rib cartilage
contributors.explanation: The cartilage joining the ribs to the breastbone can get irritated, causing pain that's tender to touch and worse with deep breaths.
contributors.ask: Is it tender when you press along the breastbone?

contributors.name: Posture and tight chest muscles
contributors.explanation: Long hours sitting with rounded shoulders tighten the chest muscles.

self_care: Rest from the movement that set it off
Gentle warmth on the sore area
Gentle chest-opening stretches once it eases
avoid: Heavy pushing or lifting until it settles
see_someone_if: Any chest pain with breathlessness, sweating, sickness, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back: call emergency services
Chest pain that comes on with effort
It doesn't settle within a few days
guides.specialist: GP (urgently if there are any warning signs)

guides.title: Abdomen

contributors.name: Digestion: indigestion, wind or constipation
contributors.explanation: Most short-lived tummy pain is linked to digestion, often related to meals, wind or constipation.
contributors.ask: Is it related to eating, or are your bowels different from usual?

contributors.name: Abdominal muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Sit-ups, lifting or twisting can strain the abdominal muscles, which hurts more with movement than at rest.
contributors.ask: Does it hurt more when you move, sit up or tense your stomach?

contributors.name: Period pain
contributors.explanation: Lower tummy cramps are very commonly linked to periods and can also be felt in the lower back.
contributors.ask: Is it linked to your period?

contributors.name: Bladder irritation
contributors.explanation: Pain low in the middle of the tummy, with burning or needing to pee often, is often linked to bladder irritation.
contributors.ask: Any burning when you pee, or needing to go more often?

self_care: Small, simple meals and plenty of water
Gentle walking often helps digestion
A warm (not hot) water bottle on the area
Note what you ate and when it hurts
avoid: Large or fatty meals until it settles
Strenuous core exercise if it's a muscle strain
see_someone_if: Severe pain, a hard swollen tummy, vomiting or blood: get urgent care
Pain with fever
It keeps coming back or lasts more than a few days
Unexplained weight loss

guides.title: Side of the body (flank)

contributors.name: Muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Twisting, lifting or sport can strain the muscles along the side of the trunk.
contributors.ask: Did it start after twisting, lifting or sport?

contributors.name: Kidney or urinary problem
contributors.explanation: Pain in the flank that comes in waves, or comes with fever or changes when you pee, can come from the kidney and needs checking.
contributors.ask: Is it with fever, or pain or changes when you pee?

contributors.name: Long sitting or one-sided posture
contributors.explanation: Sitting or standing leaning to one side for long periods loads the muscles on that side.

self_care: Gentle movement and side stretches if it's muscular
Warmth on the area
Drink plenty of water
avoid: Heavy lifting and twisting until it settles
see_someone_if: Fever, chills, or pain or blood when you pee: see a doctor today
Pain coming in strong waves
It doesn't settle within a few days

guides.title: Lower back

contributors.name: Muscle or ligament strain
contributors.explanation: Lifting, bending or a sudden twist commonly strains the muscles and ligaments of the lower back. This is the most common cause of lower back pain and usually settles within a few weeks.
contributors.ask: Did it start during or after lifting, bending or a workout?

contributors.name: Long periods of sitting
contributors.explanation: Sitting for hours, especially slumped, loads the lower back and is a very common reason for an aching, stiff back.
contributors.ask: Is it worse after sitting for a long time?

contributors.name: Irritated nerve (sciatic or lumbar)
contributors.explanation: When a disc or joint in the lower spine irritates a nerve root, pain can travel into the buttock or down the leg, often with tingling or numbness.
contributors.ask: Does it travel into your buttock or down your leg, or come with tingling?

contributors.name: Stiff spinal joints
contributors.explanation: The small joints in the lower spine can get stiff and sore, often worse in the morning or when leaning back.
contributors.ask: Is it stiffest in the morning or worse when leaning back?

contributors.name: Weak core and hip muscles
contributors.explanation: When the deep core and glute muscles aren't doing their share, the lower back takes extra load, especially with lots of sitting.

contributors.name: Period-related back pain
contributors.explanation: Lower back ache is commonly linked to periods.
contributors.ask: Is it linked to your period?

self_care: Keep moving gently: short walks help more than bed rest
Warmth on the lower back
Break up sitting every 30–45 minutes
Gentle stretches like knees-to-chest or child's pose, within comfort
Sleep on your side with a pillow between the knees
avoid: Heavy lifting or twisting until it settles
Long periods sitting without a break
see_someone_if: Numbness around the groin or bottom, or new bladder or bowel problems: get emergency care
Leg weakness
It started after a fall
No improvement after 4–6 weeks

guides.title: SI joint and buttock

contributors.name: SI joint irritation
contributors.explanation: The joint where the spine meets the pelvis can get irritated, causing pain just to one side of the base of the spine, sometimes spreading into the buttock or groin.
contributors.ask: Is it worse standing on one leg, climbing stairs or getting out of a car?

contributors.name: Tight glute or piriformis muscle
contributors.explanation: Tight muscles deep in the buttock are commonly linked to buttock ache, and can press on the sciatic nerve.
contributors.ask: Is it worse after sitting, or ease with stretching the buttock?

contributors.name: Irritated sciatic nerve
contributors.explanation: Pain from the lower back can travel into the buttock and down the leg along the sciatic nerve, often with tingling.
contributors.ask: Does it travel down the back of your leg or come with tingling?

contributors.name: Pregnancy or recent birth
contributors.explanation: Pelvic joints loosen in pregnancy and after birth, which commonly causes SI joint and buttock pain.

self_care: Keep moving gently; short walks
Gentle glute and hip stretches
Warmth on the area
Avoid sitting on hard surfaces for long periods
avoid: Long sitting on hard seats
Standing on one leg (e.g. putting trousers on) — sit down instead
see_someone_if: Numbness around the groin or bottom, or bladder or bowel changes: get emergency care
Leg weakness
No improvement after 4 weeks

guides.title: Hip

contributors.name: Irritated tendons on the outside of the hip
contributors.explanation: The tendons over the bony point of the hip commonly get irritated, hurting when lying on that side, climbing stairs or standing on one leg.
contributors.ask: Is it sore lying on that side at night?

contributors.name: Tight or strained hip flexors
contributors.explanation: The muscles at the front of the hip tighten with lots of sitting and can be strained by running, kicking or sprinting.
contributors.ask: Is it worse lifting your knee or after sitting?

contributors.name: Hip joint irritation or wear
contributors.explanation: Pain deep in the hip or groin, with stiffness putting on socks or getting out of a car, is commonly linked to the hip joint, especially from middle age.
contributors.ask: Is it stiff putting on socks or getting out of a car?

contributors.name: Pain coming from the lower back
contributors.explanation: Lower back problems can refer pain into the hip and outer thigh.
contributors.ask: Is your lower back sore too?

self_care: Keep moving within comfort
Sleep with a pillow between your knees
Gentle hip stretches and glute strengthening once it eases
Ice after activity or warmth for stiffness
avoid: Lying on the sore side
Crossing your legs or standing with weight on one hip
see_someone_if: You can't put weight on the leg
It started after a fall
Fever with a hot, swollen joint
No improvement after 2–3 weeks

guides.title: Groin and inner thigh

contributors.name: Strained inner-thigh muscle
contributors.explanation: Sports with quick changes of direction, kicking or stretching wide commonly strain the inner-thigh (adductor) muscles.
contributors.ask: Did it start with sport, kicking or a sudden stretch?

contributors.name: Hip joint
contributors.explanation: The hip joint sits right behind the groin, so hip problems often show up as groin pain.
contributors.ask: Is it stiff or sore when you turn your leg in or squat?

contributors.name: Pain coming from the lower back or SI joint
contributors.explanation: Nerves from the lower spine supply the groin, so lower back or SI joint problems can be felt here.
contributors.ask: Have you had lower back pain recently?

contributors.name: Hernia
contributors.explanation: A bulge in the groin that's sore when coughing or lifting is often a hernia and should be checked by a doctor.
contributors.ask: Is there a lump or bulge that's sore when you cough or lift?

self_care: Rest from the sport or movement that set it off
Ice for 15 minutes after activity in the first days
Gentle inner-thigh stretches once it eases
avoid: Sprinting, kicking and quick changes of direction until it settles
see_someone_if: A lump in the groin
Testicular pain or swelling: get urgent care
Fever, or pain with peeing
No improvement after 2 weeks

guides.title: Thigh

contributors.name: Muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Sprinting, kicking or a sudden stretch commonly strains the hamstring (back) or quadriceps (front) muscles.
contributors.ask: Did it start suddenly during sport or a sprint?

contributors.name: Overuse or a jump in training
contributors.explanation: A sudden increase in running, cycling or leg training often leaves the thigh muscles sore.
contributors.ask: Have you increased your training recently?

contributors.name: Irritated nerve from the back
contributors.explanation: Tingling or burning in the thigh is often linked to an irritated nerve coming from the lower back.
contributors.ask: Is there tingling, numbness or burning?

contributors.name: Tight band on the outside of the thigh
contributors.explanation: The tissue band down the outside of the thigh (IT band) commonly gets sore with running or cycling.

self_care: Rest from sprinting or heavy leg work for a few days
Ice in the first 2 days, then gentle warmth
Gentle stretching and gradual return to activity
avoid: Sprinting or stretching hard into pain
see_someone_if: Large bruising or a dent in the muscle
Calf or leg swelling with warmth (get checked today)
No improvement after 2 weeks

guides.title: Knee

contributors.name: Overload around the kneecap
contributors.explanation: Pain around or behind the kneecap, worse on stairs, squats or after sitting with bent knees, is very commonly linked to overload of the kneecap joint.
contributors.ask: Is it worse going down stairs, squatting or after sitting with bent knees?

contributors.name: Weak hip and glute muscles
contributors.explanation: When the hip muscles don't control the thigh well, the knee takes extra load, which is a common reason for knee pain in runners.

contributors.name: Tight IT band
contributors.explanation: Pain on the outside of the knee during running or cycling is often linked to the tissue band on the outside of the thigh.
contributors.ask: Does it come on partway through a run or ride?

contributors.name: Twisting injury (cartilage or ligament)
contributors.explanation: A twist, especially with clicking, locking or swelling, can irritate the knee cartilage or ligaments and should be checked.
contributors.ask: Did you twist it, or does it click, lock, give way or swell?

contributors.name: Joint wear
contributors.explanation: Stiffness and aching that's worse in the morning and after activity is commonly linked to joint wear, especially from middle age.

self_care: Reduce the activity that hurts rather than stopping completely
Ice for 15 minutes after activity
Strengthen thighs and hips gradually once it eases
Supportive footwear
avoid: Deep squats, kneeling and running downhill until it settles
see_someone_if: It locks, gives way or swells quickly
You can't put weight on it
Calf swelling with warmth (get checked today)
No improvement after 2–3 weeks

guides.title: Shin and calf

contributors.name: Shin overload (shin splints)
contributors.explanation: Pain along the inside of the shin is commonly linked to a sudden increase in running or jumping.
contributors.ask: Did you recently increase running or jumping?

contributors.name: Calf strain
contributors.explanation: A sudden push-off, like a sprint or jump, commonly strains the calf muscle, often felt as a sharp pull.
contributors.ask: Did you feel a sudden pull during sport?

contributors.name: Cramps
contributors.explanation: Calf cramps are common, especially at night or after exercise, and are often linked to tired muscles or dehydration.
contributors.ask: Does it come as sudden, tight cramps?

contributors.name: Tight calves
contributors.explanation: Tight calf muscles commonly ache after walking, running or long periods on your feet.

self_care: Rest from running for a few days and return gradually
Ice after activity
Gentle calf stretches
Supportive, cushioned footwear
avoid: Jumping and hard running until it settles
see_someone_if: One calf swollen, warm or red: get checked today (possible clot)
Pain in one spot on the shin bone that's sore to press (possible stress fracture)
No improvement after 2 weeks

guides.title: Foot, ankle and heel

contributors.name: Irritated tissue under the heel (plantar fascia)
contributors.explanation: Heel or arch pain that's worst with the first steps in the morning is very commonly linked to the plantar fascia.
contributors.ask: Is it worst with your first steps in the morning?

contributors.name: Achilles overload
contributors.explanation: Pain at the back of the heel or above it, stiff in the morning and after rest, is often linked to Achilles tendon overload.
contributors.ask: Is the back of your heel stiff in the morning?

contributors.name: Ankle sprain
contributors.explanation: Rolling the ankle commonly stretches the ligaments on the outside, causing pain and swelling.
contributors.ask: Did you roll or twist your ankle?

contributors.name: Footwear
contributors.explanation: Unsupportive, tight or worn-out shoes are a common, simple contributor to foot pain.

contributors.name: Tight calves
contributors.explanation: Tight calves pull on the Achilles and plantar fascia, which is commonly linked to heel and arch pain.

self_care: Supportive, cushioned shoes; avoid going barefoot on hard floors
Gentle calf and arch stretches, especially before the first steps of the day
Roll your arch over a cold bottle
Ease back on running or long standing
avoid: Walking barefoot on hard floors
Running or jumping into pain
see_someone_if: You can't put weight on it or it looks deformed after an injury
Rapid swelling, redness and heat
Numbness in the foot
No improvement after 2–3 weeks

guides.title: Upper arm

contributors.name: Muscle strain
contributors.explanation: Lifting, carrying or gym work commonly strains the biceps or triceps.
contributors.ask: Did it start after lifting, carrying or the gym?

contributors.name: Pain from the shoulder
contributors.explanation: Shoulder tendon problems commonly cause an ache in the outer upper arm.
contributors.ask: Does it hurt more lifting your arm to the side?

contributors.name: Irritated nerve from the neck
contributors.explanation: Tingling, burning or pain running down the arm is often linked to an irritated nerve in the neck.
contributors.ask: Is there tingling or numbness, or neck pain too?

self_care: Rest from the lifting that set it off
Ice after activity, warmth for stiffness
Gentle movement within comfort
avoid: Heavy lifting until it settles
see_someone_if: Arm pain with chest pain, breathlessness or sweating: call emergency services
A sudden pop with bruising or a bulge in the upper arm
Weakness or numbness
No improvement after 2 weeks

guides.title: Elbow

contributors.name: Overloaded forearm tendons (tennis or golfer's elbow)
contributors.explanation: Repeated gripping, lifting or mouse and keyboard work commonly overloads the tendons that attach at the elbow.
contributors.ask: Is it worse gripping, lifting a kettle or using a mouse?

contributors.name: Irritated nerve at the elbow
contributors.explanation: Tingling into the ring and little fingers, especially when the elbow is bent for a long time, is often linked to the nerve at the inner elbow.
contributors.ask: Do your ring or little fingers tingle?

contributors.name: Knock or bruise
contributors.explanation: A knock to the elbow can leave it sore for a while.

self_care: Ease off the gripping or lifting that triggers it
Ice after activity
Lift with palms up and keep the wrist straight
Check your mouse and keyboard setup
avoid: Repetitive gripping and heavy lifting with the wrist bent
see_someone_if: Swelling, heat and redness
It started after a fall
Numbness or weakness in the hand
No improvement after 3–4 weeks

guides.title: Forearm, wrist and hand

contributors.name: Repetitive strain
contributors.explanation: Long hours typing, using a phone or doing repetitive hand work commonly overloads the forearm and wrist tendons.
contributors.ask: Is it worse after typing, phone use or repetitive work?

contributors.name: Pressure on the nerve at the wrist
contributors.explanation: Tingling or numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often at night, is commonly linked to pressure on the nerve through the wrist.
contributors.ask: Do your thumb and first fingers tingle, especially at night?

contributors.name: Stiff or worn finger joints
contributors.explanation: Aching, stiff finger or thumb joints, worse in the morning, are commonly linked to joint wear, especially from middle age.
contributors.ask: Are your finger joints stiff in the morning?

contributors.name: Wrist sprain
contributors.explanation: A fall onto the hand or a sudden twist can sprain the wrist.
contributors.ask: Did you fall onto your hand or twist your wrist?

self_care: Take regular breaks from typing and phone use
Keep wrists straight; check your desk setup
Gentle wrist and finger stretches
A wrist splint at night can help tingling
avoid: Long unbroken typing or gaming sessions
see_someone_if: Pain after a fall onto the hand (possible fracture)
Numbness or weakness that doesn't go away
Hot, red, swollen joints
No improvement after 2–3 weeks

guides.title: Throat

contributors.name: Cold or throat infection
contributors.explanation: A sore throat is most often from a viral infection and usually settles within a week.
contributors.ask: Any cold, fever, or soreness when swallowing?

contributors.name: Front-of-neck muscle strain
contributors.explanation: The muscles at the front of the neck can get sore with posture, coughing or strain.

self_care: Warm drinks and rest
Drink plenty of water
avoid: Smoking and very hot or spicy food until it settles
see_someone_if: Difficulty breathing or swallowing: get urgent care
It lasts more than a week
Throat or neck pain with chest pain or breathlessness: call emergency services
